course_details.Overview of class: This is an audience-centered course in media studies. It will focus on and examine three modalities of media reception: seeing, listening, reading. These three modalities, while distinct and independent to a degree, are deeply interconnected. For instance, the physical act of reading involves visually following graphemes or letters on paper or on screen, and occasionally, hearing oneself read. Our focus in this course, however, is socio-cultural. We will explore how audiences engage in acts of "seeing, listening, reading" within a given media ecology, which in turn is shaped by larger societal forces, especially capitalist market economy and the new technologies of information and communication. This course will also offer a historical perspective on how our modes of perception, of which acts of seeing, listening, and reading are integral parts, have changed noticeably since the onset of modernity (however one might date it) and how they continue to change in the present.

course_details.Overview of class: This seminar examines the power of persuasion through speech, writing, and media, with a particular emphasis on performance and cinema as influential forms of communication. We will explore how creators employ spoken language, written text, and visual imagery to shape opinions and construct narratives that are both persuasive and resonant with audiences. Through the lens of film and media, students will critically analyze rhetorical strategies, framing techniques, and storytelling structures that make communication compelling and impactful. The course integrates theory and practice: students will engage with readings, class exercises, and media-making assignments designed to strengthen their persuasive communication skills. This project-based seminar emphasizes active participation through discussions, written reflections, and creative projects that experiment with a range of persuasive modes and techniques.

course_details.Overview of class: Black Social Dances Go Viral invites students into the history of Black social dances and their viral spread in the past and present. Students will learn both dance and social media history as well as how they conspire to make some of the most viral media moments of before and today. We will discuss the erasure of Black choreographers from their art form and resistance movements that have reshaped our media landscape.

course_details.Overview of class: Occurring simultaneously with a first-year research award, this weekly seminar provides a structured approach to understanding the processes of academic research investigations. This course supplements the topic-specific experiential learning occurring with a faculty research mentor. Through short readings, discussions, class speakers, and preparation of research presentation materials, students learn how to approach the problem of a research question, the ways investigative techniques contribute to knowledge production and new understandings, and how to communicate findings. Each session offers strategies for improving the research experience, understanding research thinking, and addressing issues that can arise in the lab or with a research project. Intended to be repeated in sequence Winter and Spring quarters.
course_details.Registration Requirements: Students must have been accepted into the SPARK program to enroll.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the two-quarter sequence associated with a first-year research award, students will:

1. Use research thinking to develop questions and frame processes to generate findings that will extend an academic conversation,
2. Develop skills of collaboration to foster inquiry and discovery,
3. Articulate research purposes with lay public and professionals in a field of interest,
4. Reflect critically on the research process and their personal development as a researcher.

course_details.Overview of class:
How does a performance become valuable? Who decides, and in whose name? This seminar treats dance, theatre and their media circulation as places where value, belonging and identity are produced, branded and contested. We move from semiotics and theories of value through branding, nation branding and institutional diversity work, to citizenship, choreopolitics and the new pressures of platforms and artificial intelligence.

London is the culminating case study. Its arts ecology is shaped by public funding, post-imperial nation branding, and very public debates about diversity and citizenship, which makes a useful contrast with the philanthropic model we know in Chicago. After ten weeks of preparation, we spend a week in London seeing performances and meeting artists, administrators and scholars at a variety of institutions.
course_details.Learning Objectives: The learning objectives for this course are for students to be able to: (1) Collaboratively assess how creative industries are structured and create value for particular global cities, (2) Experiment with different media formats to demonstrate how creative work differs across transnational contexts, and (3) Explore how global, digitally connected markets impact media making groups, movements, and cultures.

The seminar involves weekly workshops of each writer's play, weekly writing assignments designed to aid
revision, and conversations around best new play development practices. Each writer will be given a faculty or
alumni mentor to act as an additional guide for revisions. Students are evaluated on their contribution to a
supportive workshop environment, their ability to meet deadlines, and the growth of their plays based on goals
they articulate early in the process.
course_details.Registration Requirements: Class attendees are based on selection by a panel of judges. Students will submit ten minute plays that will be evaluated based on plot, strength of characters, and overall writing. A panel consisting of the ten minute teachers, Laura Schellhardt and Julie Marie Myatt will pick 5 plays, and those students will be a part of this class.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
- Discuss each writer's work in a generative and supportive manner.
- Identify opportunities for improvement in their own work
- Practice the craft of creative workshops among peers.
- Navigate the writer's involvement in director selection and casting
- Communicate with directors and actors during the rehearsal process
- Showcase their work for an audience of peers and professionals
course_details.Class Materials (Required):
I Am Not Batman by Marco Ramirez
3:59 Drag Race by Marco Ramirez
Additionally, various 10 minute plays will be brought in by students, and it will be required that they are read
before class for discussion of techniques used in the plays.

course_details.Overview of class: CMN 398 SoC Capstone: a topic-based, post-graduation-focused course. In the capstones, instructors from the School of Communication, along with faculty, alumni, and professionals, leverage their expertise to guide students in exploring and navigating careers, further education, and other post-graduation opportunities within communication arts and sciences. Through collaborative efforts with instructors, peers, and guest speakers, students engage in discussions about trends, skills, and best practices of their chosen path. These courses encourage students to delve into their undergraduate journey and reflect on the knowledge, skills, values, and relationships they have acquired. Students will construct a comprehensive portfolio showcasing how their experiences align with the demands of their chosen post-graduation path, effectively demonstrating their qualifications and accomplishments.
course_details.Registration Requirements: Enrollment is restricted to SoC juniors and seniors.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Learning Goal: Explore and reflect on knowledge, skills, values, and relationships gained through coursework, internships, research, independent studies, employment, personal experience, and creative and co-curricular activities as they relate to the student's chosen post-graduate path/field. Potential Learning Outcome: Reflect on and articulate how at least two skills, values, or relationships developed or refined during your time at Northwestern connect to the skills, values, or relationships needed for your chosen post-graduate path or field. Learning Goal: Collaborate with instructor, peers, and guest speakers to identify and discuss field-specific trends, skills, and best practices. Potential Learning Outcome: Describe at least three trends, skills, or best practices in your chosen path or field. Learning Goal: Construct a portfolio to demonstrate how student's experiences, transferable skills, and accomplishments apply to the knowledge, skills, values, and best practices of their chosen field/path. Potential Learning Outcome: Construct a portfolio which includes a tailored introduction and at least two relevant artifacts or examples of skills to demonstrate understanding of your chosen field/path.
course_details.Enrollment Requirements: Enrollment Requirements: Reserved for Juniors & Seniors
